sections.text: Introduction

This document outlines the testing procedures P1, which must be performed on a 
 monthly basis ( more than once ) as indicated by M1 in the above title.

This method is applicable to steam condensate, boiler feed water and 
 industrial water having a low level of dissolved oxygen concentration.

This document initiated by Chem. Gihan Abd EL-Samee Elsaiad & reviewed by 
 department director Chem. Maha Mohamed Saad Hamouda, revised by quality 
 control Chemist Saad Sadeek Hasanen at EDEPCo, and approved by Eng: Awad M. 
 Fatthy Head Sector of Talkha Power Station.
Significance

This 
 test is carried out for dissolved oxygen measurements in closed cooling water 
 cycles and industrial waters with low level of oxygen content.

Summary of 
Method

The sample is 
 collected in a BOD bottle. The free iodine liberated in an amount equivalent 
 to the oxygen in the sample is titrated with thiosulfate using starch as an 
 indicator.
Interferences

Reducing and oxidizing materials in the sample will interfere in this method. 
 The former leads to low results and the latter to high results. 
 The use of the proper amount of alkaline iodide will minimize error from 
 reducing interferences.

Nitrite 
 interferences are eliminated by routine use of sodium azide. Ferric iron 
 interferes unless 1 ml of potassium fluoride solution is used, in which case 
 100 to 200 mg/l can be tolerated. Ferrous iron interference is eliminated by 
 the use of potassium permanganate solution.

Safety 
Precautions

items: Make sure the sample bottle is correctly labeled.
Make sure the sample bottle is free from dust and dirt.

The sample must be kept away from exposure to direct 
 sunlight.

The bottles used for BOD should be equipped with glass 
 stopper that are ground to a point to prevent trapping of air when the stopper 
 is inserted.

sections.text:
Tools and 
Equipment
Apparatus

Sample Bottle:
 One 300 ml BOD bottle having a raised lip around the neck and a glass stopper 
 ground to a conical lower tip.

Pipette: 
 2 ml transfer pipette, and serological pipettes of 1.00 and 5.00 ml capacities 
 graduated in 0.01 and 0.10 ml divisions, respectively.

Beaker: 
 1-liter beaker.

Buret: 
 10-ml buret with 0.01-ml divisions.
Reagents

Manganous Sulfate Solution, MnSO4.H2O 
 (364g/liter)- Dissolve 364 g of manganous sulfate in water, 
 filter and dilute to1 liter. No more than a trace of iodine should be 
 liberated when the solution is added to acidified (KI) solution.

Potassium Iodide, Alkaline Solution (150g/liter)- Dissolve 700 g of potassium hydroxide KOH 
 in sufficient water to make approximately 700 ml of solution in a 1 liter 
 volumetric flask and cool to room temperature. Dissolve 150 g of iodate-free 
 KI, in 200 ml of water and mix with KOH solution in the volumetric flask. 
 Dilute to approximately 900 ml with water, allow to cool and then add 10 g of 
 sodium azide NaN3 dissolved in 40 ml water, dilute to 1 liter, mix, 
 and store in a dark, rubber-stoppered bottle.

Sodium ThioSulfate Standard Solution ( 0.1N ), Dissolve 24.82 g of Na2S2O3.5H2O 
 in boiled and cooled water and diluted to 1L. Preserve by adding 5 ml of 
 chloroform. For a dilute standard titrating solution (0.005 N ) 
 transfer 25.00 ml of 0.1 N Na2S2O3.5H2O 
 to a 500-ml volumetric flask. Dilute to the mark with water and mix 
 completely.Do not prepare more than 12 to 15 h before use.
Starch Solution

Sulfuric Acid (3:1) Conc- Pour carefully 750 ml of concentrated sulfuric 
 acid (H2SO4,sp gr 1.84 ) into 250 ml of water in a 
 beaker. Cool to room temperature, transfer to a 1 liter volumetric flask, and 
 dilute to the mark with water.
Purity of Water

All reagent 
 should conform to the specifications of the committee on Analytical reagents 
 of the American chemical society where such specifications are available. 
 Other grades may be used, provided that the reagent is of high purity to 
 permit its use without lessening the accuracy of the determination.
Work to be Carried out
Sampling

Collect the sample in a 300 ml BOD bottle in 
 accordance with the sampling below:
 Place the 
 sampling vessel in the sampling bucket and collect the sample under water 
 using stainless steel or glass tubing and short pieces of neoprene tubing for 
 connections where required. Do not use copper tubing or long sections of 
 rubber tubing.

Adjust the 
 sample flow between 500 and 1000 ml /min maintaining sample temperature below 
 70oF (21oC) and below room temperature. Reduce the 
 sample flow to 100 to 200 ml /min when using 60 ml sample tubes. Introduce the 
 flowing sample into the bottom of a scrupulously clean sample vessel with a 
 small tube. Spin the sample vessel several times to dislodge air bubbles or 
 film adhering to the glass wall. Allow the sample to continue overflowing from 
 the vessel for several more minutes.

Wet the 
 stopper and then slowly withdraw the glass tube while the sample continues to 
 flow through it. As soon as the tip of the tube clears the liquid surface, 
 ease the stopper into the neck and let it float down into its seat.

Twist the stopper in tight, invert the bottle and inspect for air bubbles, if 
 any can be seen, discard the sample and collect another.

sections.text: Fixing

Fill a 2 ml transfer pipette with alkaline 
 potassium iodide solution, and with the pipette filled to the tip so that no 
 bubble of air will be forced into the sample, ease the bottle stopper out of 
 its seat and simultaneously thrust the pipette tip past it and into the neck 
 of the bottle.

Allow the contents of the pipette to drain 
 into the bottle and as the level in the pipette approaches that in the bottle 
 raise the pipette out of the bottle and let the stopper fall back into its 
 seat.

Fill 
 another 2 ml pipette with MnSO4 solution and add this to the sample 
 in the same way. Seat the stopper tightly, and shake or rotate the bottle to 
 mix the contents thoroughly. Allow the bottle to stand, when the precipitate 
 has settled below the shoulder of the bottle add 2 ml of H 2SO4 
 (3+1). In the same way seat the stopper and shake until all the precipitate is 
 dissolved.

Fixing 
 should be completed within 15 min after sampling.

sections.text:
Titration of 
Sample

Empty the cup around the stopper of the bottle 
 and wash it with water. If the temperature of the sample is above 70oF 
 (21oC), cool it by immersing the bottle in a bath of cracked ice.

Drain the sample which shall be at temperature 
 not above 70oF (21oC), into the clean beaker and add 10 
 drops of Starch indicator solution. Fill the burette in accordance with the 
 volume required for the titration, with (0.005 N) Na2S2O3 
 solution. Start the motor stirrer if available; otherwise, stir constantly 
 with a clean glass rod.

Titrate to the disappearance of the blue, 
 starch iodine color, rinsing the tip of the burette in the sample after each 
 addition as the end point approaches. Complete titration within 30 min after 
 sampling.

sections.text: Calculation

1. Calculate 
 the dissolved oxygen content of the sample in parts per million as follows:

Dissolved 
 Oxygen, ppm = 8000NS/V
Where:

N = 
 normality of the Na2 S2O3 Solution 
 (normality 0.005N),

S = 
 milliliters of Na2 S2O3 Solution required 
 for titration, and

V = 
 milliliters of sample used.

2. State the 
 method used when reporting result.
Precision

Where this 
 method is applicable, an experienced analyst can obtain results with a 
 precision of 0.002 ppm of Oxygen.
